title: Personal Velocity
full_review:
A raw, provocative and ultimately hopeful drama, "Personal Velocity" (United Artists) examines the lives of three very different women in various stages of personal crises and transcendence.

Writer-director Rebecca Miller brings her book of short stories to the screen focusing on three portraits of women who are dealing with the emotional complexities of promiscuity, violence, ambition, infidelity, family and the search for self.

In Delia (Kyra Sedgwick) the filmmaker zooms in on a claustrophobic scene of domestic violence with a woman, her husband and three children, giving it a realistic, unsettling effect. From an almost satiric narrative voiceover we learn that Delia, who had been raised by her pot-smoking, violence-prone hippie father, turned to sex at age 12 as a diversion and a means of empowerment.

The telling of Delia's story is as crude as the character's manner. The director walks a fine line between comedic irony and revealing the seriousness of a battered woman in denial. Delia is a desperate soul full of self-loathing. Her only goodness seems to be as a devoted mother whose children maintain a certain innocence given the bitter reality of their not having a stable place to live.

Greta (Parker Posey) is the centerpiece story and the most richly drawn character. Once a promising law student, following in the footsteps of her celebrity lawyer father, she drops out of school when she learns her father is leaving her mother for a younger woman. She turns her back on her Jewish heritage and marries a handsome Protestant man. After an unexpected promotion that puts her in touch with her driving ambition, she reconnects with her father, flirts with infidelity and ultimately questions her commitment to her marriage and her husband's simple ways.

Paula (Fairuza Balk) is a young woman who two years earlier ran away from home and was rescued from living on the streets by a Haitian man who becomes her boyfriend. But Paula drives off on the run again, not sure where she is going after fighting with her boyfriend over her unwanted pregnancy. Along the way she picks up a scared young hitchhiker, tells her mother about an accident that could have killed her, and concludes that the events of the past 24 hours are a sign that she must nurture the life growing within her as precious.

Using a narrative voiceover and other storytelling devices, Miller carves out three very real portraits that are both fascinating and painful to watch as she digs deep under the skin, into these women's uncertainty and their pain.

They all come out a little stronger, but are still struggling to make sense of who they are, who they can trust, and what they should be doing next. Though occasionally cynical in tone, the film ends on a somewhat uplifting note depicting the heartening effect that a new life has in grounding a young woman's own life.

None of the women portrayed is a role model. Each is very flawed and human. Nevertheless, within each woman's story there is a hope, coming from within and through a sense of family, that keeps them striving for a better life.

Some may find the frank sexual content disturbing, although it can be seen as the filmmaker's effort at honest, deglamorized portraits of women.

Because of numerous sexual encounters, brief violence, recurring rough language and some profanity, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-IV -- adults, with reservations. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
